body.text: Markets live updates: Inflation data jumps higher than expected, ASX opens lower
Two weeks out from the next Reserve Bank meeting, inflation has jumped higher than expected to 4.9 per cent while trimmed mean is at 3.8 per cent.
Wall Street's rally has spluttered to a halt with renewed selling of AI-related stocks dragging market sentiment down, including Anthropic, which has fallen below its listing price.
The ASX has opened lower and is heading for its eighth losing session out of the past nine, while October CPI data is forecast to show inflation will jump again, driven by higher fuel prices.
Follow the day's financial news and insights from our specialist business reporters on our live blog.
Disclaimer: this blog is not intended as investment advice.
Submit a comment or question
Live updates
Inflation is at its highest rate in three years
The annual rate of headline inflation surged to 4.9% in October, up from 4.3% in September.
It is the highest rate of inflation in three years, with housing, fuel, and electricity prices driving inflation higher in the last 12 months.
The annual rate of underlying inflation rose to 3.8%, up from 3.6%.

ASX climbing back from CPI shock
The ASX has clawed back some of its sharp dip in the immediate aftermath of the inflation data but is still well down for the session.
At 1:30pm, the ASX 200 was down 0.5% to 8,682 points, only marginally lower than its level before the ABS dropped the data.
However, it is still one of the better performers across Asia with Japan’s Nikkei down 3.2% and South Korea’s Kospi shedding 6.2%. China’s Shanghai Composite is down 0.8%.
The market has been dragged down by the two heavyweight sectors, the miners and the banks, while healthcare and energy have outperformed.
The miners have been hit by slump in their key commodity prices overnight, particularly copper which dropped about 5% on the LME overnight.
Copper pure play Capstone is down almost 6%, while heavyweights BHP and Rio Tinto have shed about 2%.
The banks gave up earlier gains on opening, although some solid performances among the insurers have limited the damage in the financial sector.
NAB and ANZ are down 1.3% and Macquarie has shed more than 2%. QBE is up 0.7%
The ASX 200’s top mover is Pro Medicus (+3.2%) after it won US FDA approval for its mammography tool.
The bottom mover is Elevra Lithium (-9.4%), which is down along with all the other major lithium miners.
Calvary buy up of 14 Healthscope hospitals approved
The competition regulator, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, has approved Calvary 's acquisition of 14 Healthscope hospitals.
The hospital group has been in receivership since May last year.

"By law, the ACCC’s assessment was limited to examining the competition impacts of the acquisition," a spokesperson said."This assessment involves considering the likely future state of competition if the acquisition does not go ahead."
"By law, the ACCC’s assessment was limited to examining the competition impacts of the acquisition," a spokesperson said.
"This assessment involves considering the likely future state of competition if the acquisition does not go ahead."

After looking at some of the high profile mooted proposals for the group including another private hospital operator and a previous proposal by the Healthscope receivers to create a not-for-profit entity (known as PurposeCo), the ACCC said it determined that the acquisition was unlikely to substantially lessen competition.

"Based on the material before it, the ACCC found that there was no real likelihood of any operator other than Calvary buying the 14 hospitals," it state."The ACCC also found that, if Calvary did not acquire these hospitals, there was not a real prospect that they would stay open and continue providing any services."
"Based on the material before it, the ACCC found that there was no real likelihood of any operator other than Calvary buying the 14 hospitals," it state.
"The ACCC also found that, if Calvary did not acquire these hospitals, there was not a real prospect that they would stay open and continue providing any services."

The regulator said it acknowledged the concerns raised by many people, including medical practitioners and community members, that some services would no longer be provided at certain hospitals if they were acquired by Calvary.
This included IVF and medical terminations because of Calvary's status as a Catholic provider.
But it found that if the sale didn't go ahead Healthscope services would close altogether.

Key Event
Inflation figures 'unwelcome but unsurprising': Chalmers
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has just released a statement responding to the October inflation figures. Inflation jumped up to 4.9% in the year to October, up from 4.3% in September.
"This is another unwelcome but unsurprising reminder of the pressure Australians are under," the treasurer said.
"October saw inflation rise in most major advanced economies and interest rates are going up around the world as a result.

"Since September, every major advanced economy has had a rate rise, and the market is pricing further rate hikes in every one of them. Inflation is still much lower than its peak in 2022 but it’s still too high.
"We had an inflation challenge in our economy before the conflict in the Middle East but the war is making it worse.
"This inflation challenge is the primary influence on the budget update we will finalise in the coming weeks and release in December."

Key Event
Construction work rises in Q3
While the smoke and cordite drifts away from the CPI detonation, it's worth remembering it wasn't the only piece of economic data dropped today.

Q3 construction work done was released at the same time as CPI, with the value of work done rising a better-than-expected 0.9% (in seasonally adjusted terms) to $88.2 billion in the three months to October.
The consensus forecast was for a 0.7% lift after the Q2 contraction.
Engineering work fell 0.9% while building work rose 2.4% in the September quarter.
Engineering work was 1.3% higher and building work done was 9.6% higher from the same time last year.
The trend estimate for total construction work done rose 2.0% in the September quarter.
RBA to mull on inflation data over summer
Indeed's Australian chief economist Callam Pickering says the RBA is unlikely to make a surprise pre-Christmas rate hike.
"While inflation is clearly too high, another rate hike this year still seems unlikely," Mr Pickering said.
The RBA board's next meeting is in a fortnight with a rates decision set down for 2:30pm Tuesday December 8.
"The RBA has already hiked five times this year and with the unemployment rate rising sharply in recent months, we expect little appetite for further tightening in December," Mr Pickering said.

"Instead, we expect the RBA to take the opportunity over summer to assess how the economy is coping with the current hiking cycle. Our view is that while inflation is still much too high, there is good reason to expect it to moderate considerably over the next six months, particularly now the job market has softened."
Key Event
Inflation high but recession, rate rises still off the cards: Deloitte
Deloitte Access Economics partner Stephen Smith says while today's inflation data is bad news, Australia is still expected to avoid a recession.
It is, however, a reminder that many households are facing higher prices, higher mortgage repayments and a weaker jobs market — meaning it already feels like the economy is in recession.

"Each increase in fuel leaves households with less to spend elsewhere," Smith said."For businesses, sustained increases in fuel costs make it more expensive to deliver goods and provide services."Some of those costs can find their way into prices well after the initial rise at the pump."
"Each increase in fuel leaves households with less to spend elsewhere," Smith said.
"For businesses, sustained increases in fuel costs make it more expensive to deliver goods and provide services.
"Some of those costs can find their way into prices well after the initial rise at the pump."
The surge in headline inflation was driven by yet another jump in fuel prices, which rose 6.3 per cent during October and 39.2 per cent since February, before the conflict started in the Middle East.
The annual rise in headline inflation was also amplified by a component of earlier electricity rebates rolling out of the base year.
Rebates pushed measured power prices down by 10.2 per cent in October 2025, meaning that electricity bills in October 2026 are being compared with an unusually low starting point.

He said although the underlying result was above market consensus, Deloitte’s view "remains that the Reserve Bank will keep interest rates on hold" when it meets next month because of this month's unexpectedly high unemployment numbers.

"The five interest rate hikes already seen this calendar year are still working their way through the economy, with the Reserve Bank likely wanting more time to judge their impact before deciding whether to go again," Smith said.
"With higher interest rates, falling house prices, weak sentiment and the unrelenting cost-of-living, a weaker labour market is setting up a challenging economic outlook for 2027."
Key Event
February hike not guaranteed despite CPI data: UBS
Here's the first hot take from the hotter-than-expected CPI data we've spotted from the key market economists.
UBS economist Stephen Wu says "the high CPI raises risk of extra RBA 25bps hike in February but dovish external board members still likely means no hike."
UBS maintains a 25 bps cut in August 2027 is still on the cards.
Key Event
RBA still expected to cut interest rates in 2027 despite worse-than-expected inflation data
Despite inflation rising to a three-year high of 4.9%, the Reserve Bank will almost certainly keep interest rates on hold at its next board meeting in December.
Financial markets are betting the RBA will leave the cash rate unchanged for the next few months, after raising them five times this year.
But with unemployment rising higher than expected, and the Australian economy facing a major slowdown, the conversation has shifted to "when will the RBA start cutting rates"?
There's a 48% chance the bank will cut rates in May next year — down from 56% before the ABS released its worse-than-expected inflation data.
That's according to Bloomberg's latest data on interest rate swaps pricing.
But in August, the probability of rate relief was still around 100%.

So the key take-out is markets are still "pricing in" rate cuts in late 2027. Especially in an economic environment that increasingly "feels like a recession" (to paraphrase RBA governor Michele Bullock).

Key Event
Financial misconduct compensation scheme faces another cost blowout
A government scheme that provides compensation for victims of financial misconduct faces a further funding shortfall.

The Compensation Scheme of Last Resort (CSLR) was introduced after the banking royal commission. It was designed to help consumers recover money when a financial firm had become insolvent or refused to pay determinations made by the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA).
But the scheme is capped at $150,000 per claim and funding for it has fallen well short of what is needed to cover victims in the recent high-profile financial collapses of First Guardian and Shield.
In July, the CSLR said the government needed to raise more than $190 million to fund all financial advice claims.
According to new figures, the FY2028 initial levy estimate has been calculated to be $215.1 million.
These funds will facilitate the CSLR processing of 1,847 claims, with the personal financial advice sub-sector accounting for 91 per cent of the claims.

CSLR chief executive David Berry said the key driver behind the FY2028 initial estimate was the increase in claims related to Shield and First Guardian, with more than 1,000 claims relating to advice provided on these funds expected to be paid in FY2028.
He said the CSLR was planning to seek a special levy for FY2028 and that the levy estimate would be completed by mid-2027.
"Unfortunately, we continue to see significant negative impact resulting from the actions of a very small element of the financial services industry," he said.
"We're seeing claimants who have lost a large proportion of retirement savings due to poor or inappropriate advice, with little to no prospect of meaningful recovery due to their stage of life."

Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino is looking to broaden the scope of the levies and who in the industry must pay them. He has said big super funds and SMSFs could also be made to pay the levy in future. More on that below.

Key Event
Housing the largest contributor to annual inflation: ABS
Here's some commentary from the ABS on the October CPI data that showed the annual rate of inflation jumped a higher than expected 4.9% in October, up from 4.3% in September.

"Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation in October, rising by 6.4 per cent compared to a rise of 5.2 per cent in the 12 months to September," ABS head of price statistics Rachael McCririck said.
"The 6.4 per cent rise in annual inflation for housing reflected increases for both electricity and new dwellings expenditure classes."
Electricity rose 25.2 per cent in the 12 months to October, up from an annual rise of 12.8 per cent to September.
"The rise in electricity reflects Commonwealth government rebates, which reduced household electricity costs last year but are no longer in place," Ms McCririck said.
New dwelling prices rose 5.1 per cent in the 12 months to October, up from an annual rise of 4.7 per cent to September. This was driven by builders passing on higher costs for materials and labour.
Transport was the second largest contributor to annual inflation in October, rising by 10.6 per cent due to higher automotive fuel prices.
"On a monthly basis, automotive fuel prices rose 6.3 per cent in October, compared to a rise of 9.4 per cent in September. This was driven by higher world oil prices," Ms McCririck said.
When prices for some items change significantly, measures like the Trimmed mean can give more insights into how underlying inflation is trending without the impact of temporary shocks.
Automotive fuel was excluded from the trimmed mean in October, and this was a key driver of the difference between headline and trimmed mean inflation.

Key Event
NAB boss blasts 'unfair and damaging' online claims
For several months, a former NAB contractor has been posting on Instagram about the experiences they and others have allegedly had with the Big Four bank.
It's ramped up in recent weeks.
The posts make explosive allegations about the culture and conduct by both senior and middle management staff.
The posts often name specific people and do not have supporting evidence to substantiate the claims. The allegations are extremely serious.
It comes at a difficult time for the bank, which is laying off 2,500 people.
CEO Andrew Irvine sent an all-staff email that noted the bank had failed to convince Meta (parent company of Facebook and Instagram) to remove the posts.

"Over recent days, a social media account has posted allegations about NAB and our people. This goes beyond (executive leadership team) and extends to colleagues throughout the bank, former colleagues, partners and even their children. We know many people are experiencing hurt and distress from these posts, and this is extremely disappointing.

"We’re focussed on caring for them, including providing specialised support. At the same time we are seeking to protect current and former NAB colleagues from further unfair and damaging posts of this kind. This includes liaising with the social media platform.
"We have offered this afternoon to meet with the individual behind the social media account to hear their specific concerns directly and understand them better."
The email goes on to acknowledge the difficult period that is "creating uncertainty" for staff.
"During this period, and always, it is important to question decisions and to speak up when something doesn't feel right. We want you to do that.
"Speaking up about concerns and possible wrongdoing is not the same as online content that contains untrue, unverified and potentially harmful allegations about individuals.
"We should be able to disagree, challenge and raise concerns while still treating each other with respect."
Do you know more? Let us know in the comments and leave your contact details.

Key Event
Titanium miner IperionX confirms it is moving out
The ASX-listed, US-focused titanium miner IperionX says it has advanced its plans to shift its headquarters to Texas.
In a statement to the ASX, IperionX said it had executed a Scheme Implementation Deed which advances the plans to redomicile it announced in August.

"Redomiciling into the United States aligns IperionX's corporate domicile with its 100% US-based operating footprint, including all manufacturing facilities, mineral assets, R&D operations and principal offices," the company said.

It also falls in line with US government policies to build up domestic titanium and critical mineral supply chains while strengthening the miner's position as a supplier of defence, aerospace, consumer electronics and automotive manufacturing, the company noted.

The new Texas based corporation, currently named US Holdco, will have a direct primary listing on Nasdaq, while Australian investors will retain local market access via CHESS Depositary Interests (CDIs) quoted on the ASX.
Key Event
Harvey Norman's grim trading update
Retailer Harvey Norman has issued a grim trading update ahead of today's AGM.
Its unaudited preliminary pre-tax profit for the period from July 1 to October 31 is down 47% compared to same period ayear ago.
Sales at Australian franchises dropped 3.7% over the same period compared to last year, while comparable sales so far in November are down 1.6% on a year ago.
The retailer noted that historically November and December have been the largest contributors to its first-half profits.
Key Event
China's Huawei convicted in US criminal trial over Iran business

Chinese telecommunications equipment maker Huawei has been convicted by a jury in New York City in a sprawling US criminal case on charges that it deceived banks about its business in Iran and stole trade secrets from American companies.

The verdict came in a criminal case that began in 2018, with the US government the following year placing Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology amid American concerns that Huawei posed national security risks.
The jury in Brooklyn federal court found Huawei guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts the company faced, including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations and conspiring to steal trade secrets.
The jury acquitted Huawei of conspiring to obstruct justice and racketeering conspiracy, a charge alleging the company had acted as a criminal enterprise.
The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defence calling 15.
It was not immediately clear what penalties Huawei will face when US District Judge Ann Donnelly sentences it on September 14, 2027.
Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, said the company was disappointed by the convictions but said the acquittal on the racketeering conspiracy charge vindicated its "good-faith compliance culture."
"We fully expect to appeal," Mr Heberlig told reporters.
The trial indictment also alleged that Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran.

Key Event
Copper resumes its fall
The industrial/base metals sector had another tough session, weighed down by concerns over AI and threats of new US tariffs being imposed against major manufacturing nations.
The overall London Metal Exchange index dropped more than 5%, dragged down by an almost 5% fall in copper prices and sharp declines in aluminium and zinc.
ANZ commodities analyst Daniel Hynes said the overall bearish sentiment in metal markets was "exacerbated by reports of US tariff set to replace levies struck down by the US Supreme Court".
"This will be focused on goods from China, the EU and more than a dozen other economies," Mr Hynes wrote in a morning note.
"The likelihood of a tariff applied to refined metal entering the US appears to be fading.
"Those concerns had led to a build-up of stock in US warehouses.
"However, logistics companies are now fielding enquiries on exporting some of the stockpiles.
"The combination of a tariff-induced slowdown in economic activity just as US stockpiles are opened up to a broader market would keep downward pressure on prices in the short term," Mr Hynes said.
Key Event
Market anxiety about new set of US tariffs set to be released

While much of the analysis of Wall Street's wobbles this morning has focused on concerns about AI, there is an undercurrent of worry about a new set of tariffs the Trump administration is set to release to replace ones previously struck down by the US Supreme Court.
Media reports suggest the new tariff announcement could come as soon as today, targeting what the White House says is the excess industrial capacity in 16 trading partners.
The tariffs, to be introduced under the 1974 Trade Act, will replace those that were struck down by the Supreme Court in February this year.
Australia is not included the 16 nations US Trade Representative's office targeted in its Section 301 investigation.
The US Trade Representative's office is expected to propose new duties that would stack on top of previous tariffs already imposed during President Donald Trump's second term.
It is unclear what tariff rates would be proposed.
Reuters is reporting one source saying that the duties would be specifically tailored to each country, with goods from Mexico and Norway unlikely to have any immediate levies.
Media reports speculate that the EU, Japan and South Korea could face tariffs of up to 15%, while tariff rates for China, Vietnam and India are expected to be higher.
"The reimposition of tariffs will add to current economic uncertainty amid affordability constraints," the ANZ's morning note said.

"Fed research shows how tariffs disproportionately hurt low and middle-income households and result in a 'pay more, buy less' outcome for most."Renewed tariffs also add to the challenges facing the FOMC as it battles to return inflation to target and keep it there."

Key Event
Nvidia's oversized importance to Wall Street
NAB's senior FX strategist Rodrigo Catril had some interesting observations in his morning note about Wall Street's unusually high sensitivity to Nvidia and the broader AI complex.
Nvidia fell about 6% this morning after surging 31% on Monday following the board's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang.

"The decision gives clarity to Nvidia's leadership, but it has also raised difficult corporate-governance and national-security issues, particularly given the reported political pressure behind his return," Mr Catril said.
"Are we now in an era where too big to fail CEOs are immune to corporate governance?

"Huang now faces congressional scrutiny, including a transcribed House interview on 1 December and a public Senate Banking Committee hearing on 3 December. The board also remains exposed to any new disclosures.
"Huang's return does not resolve the larger questions hanging over the AI trade which is not just driving US equities but is also a key growth engine for the US economy.

"Investors are still assessing whether data-centre investment will generate adequate revenues, whether lenders and capital-market investors will continue financing the build-out, and whether tighter chip controls or regulation will constrain growth.
"The US government is clearly backing the AI trade and its key players, but its unclear whether a Blue Congress will show the same kind of support."
Aussie dollar and inflation
The Aussie dollar rose about 0.3% overnight to near 0.6640, supported by a lower US dollar, which was down about 0.6% against a basket of currencies of its major trading partners.
As the CBA morning currency note points out, weaker risk sentiment weighed on AUD against most of the other major currencies.
The Australian CPI for October will be the focus in our time zone.
CBA's economics team estimates trimmed inflation increased by a strong 0.3%/month in October, slightly below consensus.

"The risk is a stronger 0.4%/month. A stronger outcome today would help push AUD/USD back up towards 0.6700," CBA FX strategy team said."We expect tonight's US PCE inflation to print on the weaker side of the consensus, which would also support AUD/USD."

Happy Consumer Price Index day – or not (October edition).
For those playing CPI bingo today, we prepared this primer for you ahead the 11:30am AEDT release from the ABS.
They are the key consensus forecasts blended from the major market economists
• Headline CPI (month-on-month): +0.4%. Previous +0.8% (Range +0.3% to +0.6%)
• Headline CPI (year-on-year): +4.8% Previous +4.3%
• Trimmed mean CPI (mom): +0.4% Previous +0.2% (Range +0.3% to +0.5%)
• Trimmed mean CPI (yoy): +3.7% Previous +3.6%
• RBA target band: 2% to 3%
Impact of fuel
Fuel is expected to be a big contributor to headline inflation with fuel prices expected to increase by more than 7% across October.
This alone would contribute around 0.3% to headline inflation and lift the annual fuel inflation rate to above 33%.
Housing
New dwelling inflation is expected to be flat while rental accommodation is forecast to rise 0.2% in original terms or 0.4% in seasonally adjusted.
Maintenance and repair costs are forecast to rise a solid 0.9% over the month, taking the yearly rate to 3.5%
Clothing, food and leisure
According to Westpac, "smaller contributions are expected from clothing & footwear (+0.06ppts), household goods & services (+0.05ppts), and meals out & takeaway (+0.04ppts).

"The main offset comes from recreation & culture (–0.18ppts), driven entirely by holiday travel (–0.18ppts), while fruit & vegetables, utilities and several other components provide only marginal offsets," Westpac forecast.
Anything else?

CBA economist Trent Saunders says the impact of the credit card surcharge will provide a one-off boost to measured inflation and will make it more difficult to assess the underlying strength of market services prices.

"Before 1 October, card surcharges were paid by consumers but excluded from the CPI because they depended on the payment method," Mr Saunders said."With businesses no longer able to levy a separate surcharge, some are likely to recover those costs through higher advertised prices, which are captured in the CPI."
"Before 1 October, card surcharges were paid by consumers but excluded from the CPI because they depended on the payment method," Mr Saunders said.
"With businesses no longer able to levy a separate surcharge, some are likely to recover those costs through higher advertised prices, which are captured in the CPI."
And the future?
The Ming Dynesty poet Wu Cheng'en once mused along the lines, "to know the future is to have changed it", but a bit of profound philosophical thinking has never worried this blog overly.

So, with that in mind we'll check out what the Westpac economics team is forecasting beyond the October data (for the record, Westpac is bang on the consensus mark with a +0.4% mom forecast for October).

"We have a preliminary estimate for the November CPI of –0.1%mth which will see the annual pace ease back to 4.6%yr. Auto fuel moved lower through November to be down –2.1% in the month with seasonal falls in garments, health, furniture & household appliances and holiday travel offsetting some strength in food, housing, communication and financial services," Westpac's senior economist Justin Smirk said.
Westpac forecasts inflation will peak in the December quarter, with inflation moderating through 2027.
Key Event
Wall Steet back in reverse as AI stocks dumped again
Heading into the final stretch on Wall Street and it looks like closing lower again despite some gains in the blue-chip Dow. AI-related stocks have dragged things down.
At 7:30am AEDT
• Nasdaq: -2.3%%

The Jensen Huang reinstatement rally at Nvidia fizzled out with the stock on course to shed about 8%, while Anthropic looks set to slip below its IPO price, which must be satisfying for all those Australian investors complaining they couldn't get a slice of the action last week.
Other chip stocks followed suit, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor index down about 9% after jumping more than 14% on Monday.
Neocloud companies also gave back some of Monday's gains, with CoreWeave and Nebius down about 13% each.
Before Monday's rebound, AI-linked stocks had struggled for weeks as investors questioned the sector's debt-fuelled spending and the returns it could generate.
Anthropic's shares tumbled 13.4% to $US76, well below their $US83 IPO price, as the AI startup's blockbuster market debut last week failed to rekindle enthusiasm for the AI trade.
Amazon and Alphabet, two of Anthropic's biggest investors, were each down about 2%.
The S&P 500 information technology index fell the most, down 3.4%.
However, defensive sectors such as health care and consumer staples rose as investors sought shelter from the AI-driven selloff, helping keep the blue-chip Dow afloat.
Locally, the ASX looks like following Wall Street lead down, but not as sharply given the paucity of AI and tech stocks trading here.
At 7:20am AEDT, futures trading on the ASX 200 pointed to a 0.2% decline today, which made it the eighth losing session in the past nine.
On commodity markets, oil was up around $US2/barrel — or 2% — as three more vessels were struck in the Strait of Hormuz.
Gold is down about 2% as expectations firmed about the Fed raising rates.
Copper is also in sharp decline down about 5% on the London Metal Exchange, giving up all of the previous sessions gains and sinking to a 13-month low.
Bitcoin has slumped back below $US60,000.
